newsitem.title: UK: Dollar finds footing after stumbling on jobs data.
newsitem.headline: Dollar finds footing after stumbling on jobs data.

text.p: The dollar steadied at midday in Europe, finding its feet after stumbling after Thursday's U.S. jobs report which dampened expectations of higher American interest rates in the near future.
The U.S. jobless rate rebounded to five percent in June from a near 24-year low of 4.8 percent in May amid a slowdown in private-sector job creation and as wage inflation remained in check.
Expectations that this would be enough to prevent the Federal Reserve from raising rates in the months ahead undermined the dollar, pushing it to a one-week low against the yen.

"We may still get a rate rise this year but I do not have as much conviction as I did before the payrolls report," said John Meisner, the manager of spot foreign exchange at Standard Chartered. "The key level for the dollar to hold above now is 1.7475 (marks)."
Dollar/yen, which earlier fell as low as 113.05, was at 113.33/43 at 1050 GMT from 113.42/52 late on Thursday in Europe. The dollar was at 1.7502/12 yen from 1.7510/15 late on Thursday.
Trading in the mark crosses, such as mark/yen and sterling/mark, has attracted more interest than the dollar in recent days, traders said.
Sterling has powered up 2.7 percent against the mark in the past three trading days, vaulting above 2.96 marks for the first time in almost six years on Thursday.
Its rise has gathered pace since the British budget presentation on Wednesday, which traders saw as leaving interest rate policy with most of the burden of curbing domestic demand.
Sterling/mark was at 2.9520/30 compared with 2.9580/90 late on Thursday in Europe.
The mark has also weakened against the yen, falling to within a whisker of the 1997 low of 64.66 it set on June 11. It was at 64.74/77 yen from 64.85/87 late on Thursday.

The key to recent broad-based mark weakness is concern about European economic and monetary union (EMU), said Sanjit Maitra, the head of economics and strategy at West LB's European treasury in London.

Speculation that the planned European single currency will be weaker and less stable than the mark has prompted some investors to increase their holdings of currencies which are not closely involved with EMU.
West LB's Maitra said fiscal tightening which the German government was having to undertake to meet the EMU criteria would hold back growth and also keep the mark soft.
Traders pushing the mark lower against other major currencies seem unlikely to encounter much resistance from the German monetary authorities, analysts said.
Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing said on Friday he saw no signs of European exchange rate tensions arising as a result of the dollar's strength.
Gerard Lyons, the chief economist at DKB International in London, is therefore targeting a mark/yen rate of 60.
"The only thing that will help the mark right now is the complete collapse of EMU," he said. "Given that this looks very unlikely, mark/yen is a one-way bet."
Japanese trade and current account statistics published on Tuesday could trigger more yen gains if they show a widening in the country's external surpluses, analysts said.
Speculation that Japanese growth has the potential to surprise on the upside will also keep the yen buoyed in the weeks ahead, they said.

Such talk meant there was limited impact after Shimpei Nukaya, a Japanese Economic Planning Agency official, said on Friday that no consideration is currently being given to raising interest rates there. At 0.5 percent, Japan's official discount rate is the lowest in the world and at a historic low.
"Japanese rates will rise and it is just a question of timing," said Meisner at Standard Chartered.
Meantime, currency trading is expected by traders to become more subdued later in Europe because of the U.S. Independence Day holiday.
--Swaha Pattanaik, London newsroom +44 171 542 6284
